archival_memory.poster_presentations: We’ve also done a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. You have to boil down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was sweating bullets. The idea of random professors or industry folks walking by, asking tough questions, really freaked me out. But it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you’re doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who showed up, and they had some interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries—like marketing analytics or even architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
archival_memory.publications: As for publications, I’ve been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I’m currently working on a larger conference submission. The bigger conference is the IEEE Visualization Conference(commonly known as IEEE VIS), which is a pretty big deal in our area. We’re focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with just a plain old 2D chart. We ran a small set of user trials—like 15 participants—recorded their times, asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire, all that jazz. Now we’re crunching the data to see if there’s a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a group effort: I’m handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, someone else is writing about the user study methodology, and our PI(principal investigator) is weaving it all into a cohesive narrative. It’s definitely a balancing act, especially since I have my senior coursework and a capstone project to manage.
archival_memory.future_plans: Sometimes I get asked if I plan on going to grad school myself. Right now, I’m leaning toward working in the industry for a couple of years—hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building—before deciding if I want to pursue a master’s or PhD. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is really tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. But I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab said that sometimes stepping into industry can give you a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, so that if you do come back for a PhD, you’ll have a more practical approach.
archival_memory.challenges_in_research: Oh, and I’d be lying if I said it’s all been sunshine and rainbows. Research can be frustrating. You’ll spend weeks on an approach that doesn’t pan out, or you’ll discover your entire idea has already been done—and improved upon—by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That part can feel like a punch in the gut. But the key is to adapt. We’ll read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, either think of a new angle or a new application, and push the boundary. That’s the essence of research. You’re never truly starting from scratch; you’re building on this giant foundation of what others have done. The sense of collaboration—both within our lab and among the global research community—is something I find really special.
archival_memory.crisis_management: One story that really stands out: a few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed. We had vital data stored there—some of which wasn’t fully backed up(I know, rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We did manage to restore most of it, but that crisis hammered home the importance of data backups. After that fiasco, we set up a better backup system, plus some checks to ensure we never again rely on a single point of failure. It was stressful, but also kind of a bonding experience for the whole lab.
archival_memory.relationship_with_professors: Another big plus is that research connects me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable; if I have a question about the direction of my career or even something I’m struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She’s been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics that was filled with academic experts from all around the world. Getting to see them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
archival_memory.future_plans_2023: Oh, wow, future plans. That’s a big topic these days, especially now that I’m in my fourth year and the finish line for undergrad is finally in sight. It’s almost comical how different my mindset is compared to freshman year—I went from thinking ‘I’ll figure out a direction eventually’ to ‘I need a solid plan or at least some prospective routes ASAP.’ Especially as a Computer Science major, there’s this unspoken pressure to land something right after graduation, whether that’s a full-time job in industry, a spot in a grad program, or some kind of startup venture. Right now, I’m leaning heavily towards going into the industry for 5 years, but I haven’t completely ruled out the possibility of grad school somewhere down the line.
archival_memory.career_goals: I guess I should start with what I’m aiming for in the job market. I’ve been exploring software engineering roles that overlap with the fields I’ve grown passionate about—data visualization, VR/AR technologies, and maybe some data-driven product development. Over the past couple of years, especially through my research experience, I’ve discovered this love for making huge datasets approachable and interactive. I keep fantasizing about how that might translate into a commercial product or even an open-source framework that can benefit a wider community. That’s one reason I’m drawn to certain tech companies known for pushing boundaries in data analytics or immersive technologies—places like Unity, Unreal, or even some lesser-known startups working on specialized VR solutions for healthcare or engineering. One of my lab mentors basically told me, ‘Follow the domain that excites you, not just the biggest name brand out there.’ That advice really clicked. Sure, the Googles, Amazons, and Facebooks(or Meta, I guess) of the world are tempting, but so are these smaller companies where I might have a bigger impact earlier on.
archival_memory.job_search_process: As for my actual search process, I’m in the thick of campus recruiting right now. We have career fairs, which can be both exhilarating and stressful. I’ve already submitted a bunch of applications, mostly for software engineering or data engineering intern-to-full-time conversion roles. Luckily, I did an internship last summer at a tech startup with 9 people that specialized in data analytics software for logistics companies. It was such a valuable experience because I got to see how a real development team operates, how they plan sprints, manage code reviews, and handle feature rollouts to actual paying clients. My tasks ranged from building small UI components for their analytics dashboard to writing data pipelines that process shipping events in near real-time. By the end of that internship, I felt more confident in my skills, and I think that’s going to help me stand out when I interview.
archival_memory.grad_school_considerations: On the grad school front: part of me is really intrigued by the idea of continuing my research in immersive analytics or even branching into human-computer interaction for large datasets. I’ve seen how advanced degrees can open doors to specialized R&D roles, either in industry labs or in academia. Writing those workshop papers and currently working on a conference submission has shown me that I do enjoy the deeper exploration of a single topic—figuring out how to push the needle forward in a meaningful way. But on the flip side, there’s a practical consideration: I’d like to apply what I’ve learned in a more commercial setting, at least for a while, before I commit another five to six years for a PhD(or even two if I go for a master’s first). Some of my peers say I could do a master’s part-time while working. Others say it’s better to go all-in if I’m going to do it. It’s honestly a lot to weigh.
archival_memory.campus_life_impact: Another big piece of this puzzle is my previous involvement in various campus clubs and projects, which has shaped how I see my future. Being part of group-driven assignments—like my current capstone project analyzing social media sentiment for emergency responses—makes me realize how much I thrive on teamwork and problem-solving in high-stakes scenarios. It’s not just about coding for me; it’s about working closely with people, brainstorming solutions, putting together prototypes, seeing them fail, and then iterating until they work. That’s exactly the type of environment I want once I graduate. I’m certain I don’t want a role where I’m locked away on tiny, siloed tasks. I’d love to end up at a company that encourages cross-functional collaboration—with designers, data scientists, product managers, or even domain experts in non-tech fields. That interdisciplinary vibe is something I’ve enjoyed a lot in my research lab, and I want it in my professional life, too.
archival_memory.financial_considerations: Financial considerations come into play as well. I’ve got some student loans, though not astronomical, but it’s enough that I’m conscious about wanting a stable income soon after I graduate. I’m not above the practicalities—health insurance, paying rent, saving up a bit. A full-time engineering position usually comes with a decent salary, which could help me knock out that debt faster. If I went straight into grad school, funding can be complicated. Some PhD programs offer stipends, some don’t. Master’s programs often require you to pay tuition, and scholarships can be competitive. So, part of me is thinking: a good job in industry could serve a dual purpose—alleviating financial strain and giving me career momentum—while I figure out if I truly want to go back to school.
archival_memory.career_timeline: The timeline is also crucial. A lot of companies do their hiring in waves, especially for new grads. I’m trying to stay on top of deadlines. There’s always interview prep to do—technical interviews can be grueling with their algorithmic challenges, system design scenarios, and even some domain-specific tests if you’re applying to specialized roles. I actually set aside at least a couple of hours each week to go through practice problems, brush up on coding patterns, revisit data structures and algorithms. I wouldn’t say I love the interview grind—who does, right?—but I get why it exists. On the bright side, the advanced courses I’m taking, like Advanced Algorithms and Distributed Systems, are directly boosting my confidence for those tech screens. I definitely notice how comfortable I’ve gotten talking about things like concurrency, big-O notation, or analyzing the trade-offs of certain architecture designs.
archival_memory.job_opportunities: A few companies have already reached out for initial chats. It’s kind of surreal to have recruiters ping you on LinkedIn, especially when you still feel like a student who’s just trying to keep your head above water with assignments. I’m trying not to get too carried away—after all, a recruiter message is just the tip of the iceberg in terms of the hiring process. But I am optimistic. There’s always that voice in my head whispering, ‘Don’t forget about Plan B, or Plan C.’ So I’m also looking into smaller companies or startups in my city or the nearby tech hubs. Sometimes those can lead to more hands-on roles where you really learn from day one. The fantasy of joining a brand-new VR startup, maybe having a stake in its success, and building out a product from scratch—that’s super appealing, especially to my entrepreneurial side.
archival_memory.entrepreneurial_aspirations: Speaking of entrepreneurship, I’ve toyed with the idea of launching something of my own. Not necessarily right after graduation—maybe that’d be too risky—but maybe after I gain enough industry experience. I’ve had a couple of ideas floating around for VR-based training simulators or interactive data analytics platforms. If I teamed up with a few talented friends from my advanced classes or from the research lab, we could potentially spin up a small venture. But that’s a big leap. I’m not naïve about how tough it is to maintain a startup, especially if there’s no guaranteed paycheck coming in. My parents have been supportive in general, but they remind me to keep my feet on the ground and consider the realities of living expenses. They’re not pushing me in any one direction, but they’ve always emphasized financial independence as a cornerstone of life after college.
archival_memory.family_and_location: Family is another factor—my folks live in a different state, and I have to think about how far I’m willing to move. Tech is obviously huge in places like Silicon Valley, Seattle, Austin, and now even in Midwest hubs, so location might come into play. I’m not opposed to relocating, but I also know that if I end up taking an offer in a city that’s too far, visiting home becomes a logistical puzzle. Some of my upperclassmen friends who graduated last year say that remote or hybrid roles have changed the game. Maybe that means I could live near family or wherever I’m most comfortable, while still working for a big name or an innovative startup. It’s a great time to be entering the tech workforce—there are so many options, though it can be a bit overwhelming to juggle them all.
archival_memory.career_goals_and_aspirations: One thing I do know for certain: I want to keep growing my skills and not get complacent. Even if I land in a role that’s not 100% perfect, as long as I’m learning—picking up new frameworks, new approaches to product development, or even new management skills—I’ll consider that a success. My biggest fear is stagnation, especially in a field that moves as fast as ours. So wherever I go, I’m planning to stay curious, keep pushing my own boundaries, and maybe carve out a niche as a specialist in immersive tech for data. That’s the goal, at least. Next steps: finish out senior year strong, keep interviewing, see which offers come my way, and hopefully make a decision by late spring. Fingers crossed that the stars align the way I’m hoping, but if they don’t, I’m confident I’ll figure it out. I’ve learned that you have to be flexible—you never know how life will unfold after you toss that graduation cap in the air. For now, I’m just excited about the potential paths ahead.
